title: Sydney Opera House
blurb: Jørn Utzon’s 1973 performing arts centre on Sydney Harbour. Its precast concrete shells are all sections of a single 75.2 m sphere, set on a granite podium.

sourceUrls.label: Sydney Opera House: Renewing an icon (official stories)
Sydney Opera House Trust: Regulatory Impact Statement (Forecourt capacity)
Sydney Opera House: visitor map (Broadwalk, Central Passage, Box Office)

systems.name: Podium
systems.description: The monumental base, 183 m long and 120 m wide, clad in pink granite aggregate panels quarried at Tarana.

systems.name: Concert Hall shells
systems.description: The western group of precast concrete shells over the Concert Hall. Each shell is a section of a single 75.2 m sphere, stepping up from low entrance shells to the high stage tower.

systems.name: Opera Theatre shells
systems.description: The eastern group of shells over the Joan Sutherland Theatre, called the Opera Theatre until 2012. Each shell is a section of a single 75.2 m sphere.

systems.name: Restaurant shells
systems.description: The smaller group of shells on the western side of the Monumental Steps, housing the Bennelong Restaurant.

systems.name: Glass walls
systems.description: Glass curtain walls enclosing the foyer spaces between the podium and the shells.

systems.name: Interiors
systems.description: Performance venues inside the podium and beneath the shells, from the 2,679 seat Concert Hall to the 210 seat Utzon Room.

systems.name: Steps and terraces
systems.description: The stone paved forecourt, the Monumental Steps, and the western broadwalk, used as an outdoor performance space.

systems.name: Structure
systems.description: The 588 concrete piers under the building, the podium columns, and the pedestals and ribs carrying the shells.

explanations.podium platform: The monumental podium measures 183 m long and 120 m wide and covers 1.8 hectares. Its exterior is clad in aggregate panels of pink granite quarried at Tarana.
explanations.podium granite paving: Granite paving tops the podium. Utzon first intended to leave the podium open down to the water; the built version was clad and paved instead.
explanations.seawall base: Schematic base at the waterline. The building stands on 588 concrete piers sunk as much as 25 m below sea level.
explanations.north podium terrace: Schematic terrace at the north end of the podium. Substantial open public spaces ring the whole podium.
explanations.south podium terrace: Schematic terrace at the south end of the podium, beside the Bennelong Restaurant shells.
explanations.podium box office level: The main Box Office Foyer sits beneath the Monumental Steps; the Opera House's own renewal notes describe a new lift and a visitor lounge added there. Interior layout is schematic.
explanations.podium concourse level: The concourse level inside the podium. The Opera House's own operational plans name the Lower Concourse, and visitor guidance describes crossing from the Forecourt to the concourse entrance. Layout is schematic.
explanations.western foyer: The western foyer of the podium. The northern and western foyers are also used for performances on an occasional basis. Foyer layout is schematic.
explanations.northern foyer: The northern foyer of the podium. The northern and western foyers are also used for performances on an occasional basis. Foyer layout is schematic.
explanations.central passage: The Central Passage runs through the podium on the Opera House's own visitor map. Layout is schematic.
explanations.concert hall auditorium: The Concert Hall seats 2,679 and is home to the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. It began as a multipurpose opera and concert hall, and the fitted stage machinery was later pulled out.
explanations.concert hall stage: The stage of the Concert Hall. The major hall was originally intended as a multipurpose opera and concert hall; the stage machinery already designed and fitted was pulled out and largely thrown away. Stage geometry is schematic.
explanations.concert hall stalls seating: Seating terraces of the Concert Hall, which seats 2,679 and is home to the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. Layout is schematic.
explanations.grand organ: The Sydney Opera House Grand Organ is the largest mechanical tracker action organ in the world, with over 10,000 pipes.
explanations.concert hall acoustic clouds: Perspex rings hung over the Concert Hall stage shortly before opening, an attempt to give the musicians better early reflections.
explanations.joan sutherland theatre auditorium: The Joan Sutherland Theatre seats 1,507 and is the Sydney home of Opera Australia and The Australian Ballet. It was called the Opera Theatre until 17 October 2012.
explanations.joan sutherland theatre stage: The stage of the Joan Sutherland Theatre, a proscenium theatre with 1,507 seats, the Sydney home of Opera Australia and The Australian Ballet. Stage geometry is schematic.
explanations.joan sutherland theatre orchestra pit: The orchestra pit of the Joan Sutherland Theatre. The pit is cramped and considered dangerous to musicians' hearing. Pit geometry is schematic.
explanations.drama theatre: The Drama Theatre seats 544. The smaller venues sit within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.playhouse: The Playhouse seats 398 and sits within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.studio: The Studio holds up to 400 people depending on configuration and sits within the podium, beneath the Concert Hall.
explanations.utzon room: The Utzon Room seats 210. Rebuilt to Utzon’s own design and opened in 2004, it holds his tapestry Homage to Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach.
explanations.yallamundi rooms: The Yallamundi Rooms, a function space hosting up to 400 people, the first new venue created inside the Opera House since the Utzon Room refurbishment of 2004. Room geometry is schematic.
explanations.recording studio: The building houses a recording studio among its other facilities. Layout is schematic.
explanations.monumental steps, lower flight: The lower flight of the Monumental Steps on the western side of the podium. Together with the forecourt they form an outdoor venue, with the steps doubling as audience seating. Step divisions are schematic.

explanations.forecourt plaza: The large stone paved forecourt beside the Monumental Steps. The Opera House Trust describes the Forecourt as an open air venue south of the shells that accommodates up to 6,000 people.

explanations.concert hall entrance shell: The low entrance shell of the western group, over the Concert Hall. Each shell is a section of a single sphere 75.2 m in radius; the 14 shells of the building would combine to form a perfect sphere. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs. Shell placement and dimensions are schematic.
explanations.concert hall entrance shell tile lid: Tile lid of the concert hall entrance shell. The tile lid carries the shells' chevron pattern of 1,056,006 tiles in two colours, glossy white and matte cream, made by the Swedish company Höganäs AB; the 120 mm square Sydney Tile took three years of development. Tile layout is schematic.
explanations.concert hall entrance shell pedestal: Schematic concrete pedestal under the concert hall entrance shell. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs; Hornibrook cast 2,400 precast ribs and 4,000 roof panels in an on site factory.
explanations.concert hall entrance shell lower ribs: Schematic lower half of the precast concrete ribs fanning from the pedestal toward the apex of the concert hall entrance shell. Hornibrook manufactured the 2,400 precast ribs in an on site factory, supporting them during construction with an adjustable steel-trussed erection arch developed by Hornibrook engineer Joe Bertony.
explanations.concert hall entrance shell upper ribs: Schematic upper half of the precast concrete ribs running to the apex of the concert hall entrance shell. The 1961 spherical solution let arches of varying length be cast in a common mould and placed adjacent to one another to form the spherical section.

explanations.bennelong restaurant shell 4: One of the smaller group of shells on the western side of the Monumental Steps, housing the Bennelong Restaurant. Each shell is a section of a single sphere 75.2 m in radius; the 14 shells of the building would combine to form a perfect sphere. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs. Shell placement and dimensions are schematic.
explanations.bennelong restaurant shell 4 tile lid: Tile lid of the bennelong restaurant shell 4. The tile lid carries the shells' chevron pattern of 1,056,006 tiles in two colours, glossy white and matte cream, made by the Swedish company Höganäs AB; the 120 mm square Sydney Tile took three years of development. Tile layout is schematic.
explanations.bennelong restaurant shell 4 pedestal: Schematic concrete pedestal under the bennelong restaurant shell 4. The shells are precast concrete panels supported by precast concrete ribs; Hornibrook cast 2,400 precast ribs and 4,000 roof panels in an on site factory.
explanations.bennelong restaurant shell 4 lower ribs: Schematic lower half of the precast concrete ribs fanning from the pedestal toward the apex of the bennelong restaurant shell 4. Hornibrook manufactured the 2,400 precast ribs in an on site factory, supporting them during construction with an adjustable steel-trussed erection arch developed by Hornibrook engineer Joe Bertony.
